Okay, Diego, present the vignette to me. Short version.
A fifty-eight-year-old farmer presents with a nonhealing lesion on his nose. It has been growing for six months.
Has he tried anything?
He has been applying an antibiotic ointment for three weeks, but the lesion has not resolved. It has bled twice.
Any pertinent negatives?
No pain, no fever, no weight loss. His past medical history is unremarkable, but he has had two lesions removed from his arms.
Good. So what is on your differential?
Basal cell carcinoma first. Squamous cell carcinoma is possible, because he has worked outdoors for forty years.
And the next best step?
A shave biopsy. We cannot narrow it down without tissue.

Every vignette on Step 3 is built the same way, and once you have seen the pattern, you read faster. Start with the last line. It tells you the task: the most likely diagnosis, or the next best step in management. Then go back to the first line: age, sex, and what the patient presents with. Now the timeline. Look at the verbs. A man who has had a rash for two years is a different patient from a man who has been scratching for two days. When you read that somebody has been applying a cream for three weeks, ask yourself why it has not worked. Then read the pertinent negatives slowly. No fever, no weight loss, no new medications. Those negatives narrow down your differential more than half of the positive findings. And if the vignette says the past medical history is unremarkable, believe it. The writers do not hide anything there. Finally, before you choose, say the diagnosis in one sentence in your head. If you cannot, you have not finished reading.

I have been following one patient for almost a year now, and she has taught me more than any review book. She is a sixty-year-old teacher, and she first came in with a small patch on her cheek that she had ignored for months. We have done two biopsies since then. The first one was unremarkable, and honestly, I relaxed. But the patch has kept growing, slowly, and she has been asking me the same question at every visit: why is it still there? That question made me go back to the workup. I have read her chart three times this month. We have changed the plan: she has had a third, deeper biopsy, and we are waiting for the result. What I have learned is simple. A normal result does not end the story. If a lesion has been changing, the patient has been right to worry, and I have been wrong to relax.
